<b>Внутренние сонные артерии</b> несут о: The internal carotid arteries carry about 80% of the brain's blood. Each enters the skull through the carotid canal, bends (the siphon) in the cavernous sinus, gives off the ophthalmic artery, and next to the optic chiasm divides into the anterior and middle cerebral arteries. A plaque where the internal carotid branches off the common carotid in the neck is a frequent cause of stroke.
<b>Передние мозговые артерии</b> идут вп: The anterior cerebral arteries run forward above the optic nerves, are joined by the anterior communicating artery, and rise into the longitudinal fissure between the hemispheres. There they curve around the corpus callosum and supply the inner surface of the frontal and parietal lobes — including the cortex that controls the leg.
<b>Средние мозговые артерии</b> — самые: The middle cerebral arteries are the largest branches of the carotids. Each runs sideways deep into the lateral sulcus and fans out over the outer surface of the hemisphere. From its first segment, thin lenticulostriate arteries rise to the basal nuclei and internal capsule (not shown in the model); their blockage causes small (lacunar) infarcts.
<b>Передняя соединительная артерия</b> —: The anterior communicating artery is a bridge a few millimeters long between the anterior cerebral arteries. If one carotid is narrowed, blood flows across it from the other. It is the most common site of aneurysms: about a third of all brain artery aneurysms are found here.
<b>Задние соединительные артерии</b> свя: The posterior communicating arteries link the carotids with the posterior cerebral arteries and close the circle at the back. Normally little blood flows through them, but when one system is blocked they become a detour. An aneurysm where the posterior communicating artery begins can press on the nearby oculomotor nerve — the eyelid droops and the pupil dilates.
<b>Позвоночные артерии</b> отходят от по: The vertebral arteries branch off the subclavian arteries, rise through the cervical vertebrae, and enter the skull through the foramen magnum. Along the medulla they give off the posterior inferior cerebellar arteries, and at the lower border of the pons they join to form the basilar artery. The vertebrobasilar system brings about 20% of the brain's blood supply.
<b>Основная (базилярная) артерия</b> леж: The basilar artery lies in a groove on the front surface of the pons. Small branches feed the pons, larger ones the cerebellum, and at the upper border of the pons it divides into the two posterior cerebral arteries. Basilar thrombosis is a severe brainstem stroke: coma or locked-in syndrome — the person is conscious and moves the eyes, but the body is paralyzed.
<b>Задние мозговые артерии</b> — конечны: The posterior cerebral arteries are the terminal branches of the basilar artery. They wind around the cerebral peduncles and supply the thalamus, the lower surface of the temporal lobe, and the occipital lobe with the visual cortex. Their blockage knocks out the opposite half of the visual field in both eyes (hemianopia).
<b>Мозжечковые артерии</b> — три пары: в: The cerebellar arteries come in three pairs: the superior arise from the top of the basilar artery, the anterior inferior from its beginning, and the posterior inferior from the vertebrals. A posterior inferior cerebellar stroke also hits the lateral medulla: dizziness, trouble swallowing, and numbness of the face on one side and of the body on the other (lateral medullary, or Wallenberg, syndrome).
<b>Передняя мозговая артерия</b> питает: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the inner surface of the frontal and parietal lobes and a strip about 2 cm wide along the upper edge of the hemisphere. This is where the motor and sensory cortex for the leg lies. Its blockage causes weakness and numbness of the opposite leg, sometimes apathy and loss of bladder control.
<b>Средняя мозговая артерия</b> питает б: The middle cerebral artery supplies most of the outer surface of the hemisphere: the motor and sensory cortex for the face and arm, and in the left hemisphere (dominant for language in most people) also Broca's and Wernicke's language areas. Its blockage is the most common major stroke: the face droops, the arm weakens, speech is impaired.
<b>Задняя мозговая артерия</b> питает за: The posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital lobe with the visual cortex, the lower surface of the temporal lobe, and the thalamus. Its blockage knocks out the opposite half of the visual field in both eyes. With a left-sided lesion there may be pure alexia: the person can write but cannot read what they have written.
<b>Тромб в левой средней мозговой.</b> В: A clot in the left middle cerebral artery. At the center of the territory flow stops, and neurons die within minutes — this is the infarct core (dark). Around it is the penumbra (orange): a little blood seeps in from neighboring arteries; the cells fall silent but stay alive. Dissolving the clot (thrombolysis) or removing it with a catheter (thrombectomy) can save the penumbra.
<b>Закупорка левой внутренней сонной при: Blockage of the left internal carotid with a complete circle. Blood reaches the left anterior and middle cerebral arteries by detours: from the right through the anterior communicating artery and from behind through the posterior communicating artery (blood flows through it in the reverse direction). If the carotid narrows slowly, its closure may go unnoticed.
<b>Та же закупорка, но соединительные ар: The same blockage, but the communicating arteries are underdeveloped — as happens in many people. There is no detour, and the infarct covers the territories of the left anterior and middle cerebral arteries — almost the whole hemisphere.
<b>Тромб в основной артерии.</b> Без кро: A clot in the basilar artery. The pons, most of the cerebellum, the thalamus, and both occipital lobes are left without blood. It is a rare but extremely dangerous stroke: without treatment, most patients die.
<b>Артериальный (виллизиев) круг</b> — к: The arterial circle (circle of Willis) is a ring of arteries on the base of the brain. The internal carotids feed it from the front, and the basilar artery, formed by the joined vertebrals, from behind. The communicating arteries close the ring, so blood can flow from one system to the other. Fewer than half of people have a complete circle. View from below, forehead on the left. Choose an artery.
<b>Бассейны</b> — участки мозга, которые: Territories are the areas of the brain supplied by each cerebral artery; their borders vary slightly from person to person. Blood supply is poorest where territories meet: when blood pressure drops sharply, infarcts arise exactly there. The lateral view shows the left hemisphere, the medial view the right one. Choose an artery or click the cortex.
<b>Кровоток восстановлен.</b> Полутень с: Blood flow restored. The penumbra is saved: these neurons will work again. The dead tissue of the core will not recover — a scar will form in its place, and neighboring areas of the cortex will gradually take over some of the lost functions.
Мозг — 2 % массы тела, но берёт пятую ча: The brain is 2% of body mass but takes a fifth of the oxygen and has almost no reserves. It is fed by four arteries linked into a ring at its base, and each area of the cortex depends on its own branch — which is why a stroke reveals so precisely where a vessel has closed.
\n <div><h2>Устройство</h2>\n:
Structure

Four arteries supply the brain: the two internal carotids (the anterior system) and the two vertebrals, which join to form the basilar artery (the posterior system). On the base of the brain their branches are linked into the arterial circle (circle of Willis). Three pairs of cerebral arteries leave the circle — anterior, middle, and posterior — and the vertebral and basilar arteries also give off the cerebellar arteries and branches to the brainstem.

The large arteries run over the surface of the brain in the subarachnoid space, and thin branches dive into the tissue. The deep parts — the basal nuclei, thalamus, and internal capsule — are fed by thin straight branches from the circle and from the first segments of the cerebral arteries.

How it works

The brain receives about 15% of the blood pumped by the heart — about 50 mL per 100 g of tissue per minute. It has almost no reserves of glucose or oxygen: without blood flow, consciousness is lost in 10–15 seconds, and within a few minutes neurons begin to die.

Brain vessels keep blood flow steady when blood pressure changes (autoregulation) and widen where neurons are working harder — this is the basis of functional MRI.

Medicine

  • Ischemic stroke (about 85% of strokes) is the blockage of an artery by a clot or embolus, often from the heart in atrial fibrillation or from a plaque in the carotid artery. Warning signs follow the FAST test — Face, Arm, Speech, Time: a drooping face, a weak arm, slurred speech; call emergency services right away.
  • Time is brain: when a large artery is blocked, about 1.9 million neurons die every minute. Thrombolysis helps within the first 4.5 hours, and thrombectomy usually within 6 hours — in some patients even later.
  • A transient ischemic attack causes stroke signs that pass on their own within minutes. It is a warning: the risk of a real stroke in the next few days is high.
  • Hemorrhagic stroke is the rupture of a vessel: bleeding into the brain (more often with high blood pressure) or rupture of an aneurysm of the circle arteries with subarachnoid hemorrhage.

Simplifications

  • The brain model is simplified; the arteries are drawn thicker, and their course and branching are schematic. Deep branches, veins, and meninges are not shown. The borders of the territories are approximate. Infarct growth is sped up: 20 minutes per second; the number of dead neurons is an average estimate for a blocked large artery of the anterior circulation; for the basilar artery it is different.
